utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom today. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel. Good morning, everyone in the courtroom. Mark Harmon, Salvatore Cannata and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Today General Perisic is represented by Gregor Guy-Smith, Boris Zorko, and myself, Novak Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Good morning, good morning, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to remind you that -- just before we come -- I come to you, Mr. Borovic, just to place on the record that we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis today. Judge Picard is involved in another case this morning, might join us a little later. Just to remind you, Mr. Borovic, that you are still bound by the declaration that you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Borovic. Just a short question on a topic we've discussed before. I asked you yesterday regarding the composition of the military office of the federal president of Yugoslavia, I asked you if there were any Legal Officers in that military office. You said you didn't remember whether there were any lawyers there. Do you remember Colonel Jovovic, who that was and what he did?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember Colonel Jovovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on then to the next area I want to discuss with you, and that's the relationship between General Perisic and the process I will call depoliticisation of the army. What was your knowledge about General Perisic's views while you were working in the office of the Chief of General Staff about any influence of politics on the army?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Perisic and those of us who were working with him in the inner circle of that office were in favour of depoliticisation and stripping any influence of political parties on military activities and offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it also a position shared by other generals of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regrettably, no, it was not shared by all the generals of the Army of Yugoslavia. Some generals wanted to become close to the party in power.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now place on the screen 65 ter 01016D. First of all, could we see the last page in B/C/S and in English to see who the author is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see here who wrote this document and what position he occupied at the time. Are you familiar with the document?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Ljubisa Velickovic was at that time commander of the air force?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a letter addressed to the Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army and it says: "Prompted by the attendance at the 3rd Congress of the SPS." What was SPS at the time?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Socialist Party of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who was its president at the time?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Lieutenant-General Blagoje Kovacevic, your deputy, and Lieutenant-General Dragoljub Ojdanic 1st Army commander, I am hereby submitting my opinion. 1, one of the fundamental orientations and characteristics of the Yugoslav Army in the process of the transformation is its consistent commitment to be free from politics and ideology." What was the reason for this letter? What were the underlying facts because I think the letter is self-explanatory?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We frequently received invitations from all political parties to attend their congresses and ceremonies. The position of the Chief of the General Staff and all of us with him was that we should not attend any ceremonies organised by political parties or any congresses of parties in power or opposition parties, or if we should attend that our attendance should be spread equally among them but mainly not to attend. That was well known to all the generals, but still General Blagoje Kovacevic and General Dragoljub Ojdanic went to this congress dressed in full uniform and their attendance was recorded by TV crews and that came across as their support to the SPS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did General Perisic react to this event and to this letter by General Velickovic?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not like it, and the letter of General Velickovic just coincided with the views of General Perisic and other high-ranking military officers who wanted the army to remain professional and neutral politically.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have an exhibit number for document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D497. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the students' protest in end 1996 and early 1997 in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember the students' protests and other protest rallies held at that time in Belgrade. All of them were an expression of dissatisfaction with the authorities ruling Serbia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: More specifically?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were unhappy with the regime of Slobodan Milosevic, that was the one party in power.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the course of these protests, did students have any contact with the General Staff? Were you involved in any way personally?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was chief -- sorry, head of the centre of military schools, a title equivalent to head master or dean, and I participated in the talks and in the issuing of public statements or communiques of the students.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the students talk to anyone before they were received by you?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before they were received by us, the students' delegation went to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. We in our office monitored the reactions of the students and the public statements, and they were extremely unhappy with the way they were received by the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It was the Ministry of the Interior, not foreign affairs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I received them once it was approved by the Chief of the General Staff, the head of the students' delegation was not Cedomir Jovanovic, it was another student whose name eludes me at the moment. Anyway, I asked who was their main representative and with whom we should talk to come to a -- some common ground and issue a public joint statement and then I ushered them into the office of the Chief of General Staff to talk to the chief and the collegium of the General Staff. They said Cedomir Jovanovic was authorised to hold talks on their behalf. I asked him if he wanted to make a draft of a communique so we could harmonise our views on it and sign it together, or if I should do it because I had more experience. They suggested that I should do it and they would sign it if they agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the gist of that gist of that press statement?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gist was that we were supporting the justified demands of the students and that the problems encountered by the students have to be resolved in a democratic way. We saw them as our military conscripts and we thought it was our responsibility to take care of them, just as we took care of other young people who sympathised with the authorities. Anyway, I ushered them in and they were received by the Chief of General Staff and all the members of the collegium. They were given soft drinks and received and we told them that if they had any objection to the draft communique, that they should state these objections then and if not then they should join us before the journalists and issue that press statement as agreed. They were very decent. They made that statement as agreed and they told the press that they were very happy with the way they were received by the office of the Chief of General Staff, unlike the Ministry of the Interior. And then followed reactions concerning the office of the Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was going to ask you about that. What were the reactions of the public and the authorities?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was immediately called by General Perisic who said that Milosevic had called him asking that we take back that press statement, but we both agreed that we were not going to do it and we were prepared to take the consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how the public reacted?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a very positive reaction, very favourable to the army. After that, the students asked that their publication called "Student" should publish an interview with me as representative of the office of the Chief of General Staff and head of the centre of military schools on the occasion of its 60th anniversary. I gave them that contribution, expressing all the views of the office of Chief of General Staff and my own views as head of the centre for military schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll now move to the last subject we are going to discuss today, and that's the relationship between General Perisic and President Milosevic at the time when Milosevic was president of Serbia and later when he was president of Yugoslavia. When you left the office of the Chief of the General Staff and became head of the centre of military schools, did you continue to keep in touch with General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Perisic took a long time appointing a new Chef de Cabinet, and every day after my working hours at the centre of military schools, I would go to the office and help with their work and I had consultations with General Perisic. Simultaneously I was connected to the computer network so that I assisted my former deputy Vlajkovic who still remained in the office to deal with anything that was necessary. So I maintained close contact with both the general and his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember while you were still working as Chef de Cabinet and later on, did General Perisic consider the possibility of leaving this position, not resigning because you cannot resign in the army, but abandoning this duty as Chief of General Staff?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a possibility that was constantly open. The late General Ratko Milovanovic told me that at the time when I was supposed to begin working as Chef de Cabinet that the Chief of General Staff found it very difficult because there was no understanding for the idea to transform the Yugoslav Army and that he was on the verge of deciding to leave this position and that he believed that we had a real soldier, a humanitarian, somebody who was good in psychology and that we shouldn't change him and bring another general to this position. Later on while I worked as Chef de Cabinet after every disagreement with President Milosevic, he was in the position in which he would have preferred to abandon his post and leave this duty to somebody else. As far as we could, we supported him but also dissuaded him from this idea and tried to reinforce his position both within the army and in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who do you mean by "we"?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the morale and information service, the generals who were of the same mind as ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why did you think that he should stay in this post? Was there anything that you were afraid of?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were afraid of what happened later, namely that generals who went to congresses and who had taken the side would come to be the heads of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who became the Chief of General Staff after the replacement of General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel-General Dragoljub Ojdanic was appointed to this position after the replacement of General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for the crisis in Kosovo, was there any difference in positions between General Perisic while he was still the Chief of General Staff and President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were disagreements about how anti-terrorist campaigns should be carried out, how the units should be commanded. The president increasingly called other generals to talk to them and issue them tasks and I think that for a time he transferred command over the Guards Brigade to someone else and to General Perisic and all of us, this seemed as if the army was no longer within the system as we envisaged it. And on every occasion, the general opposed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was President Milosevic's position at the time, let us just be more specific?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the Supreme Defence Council all along, so as long as Yugoslavia existed. He was the president of the republic which made up 95 per cent of this Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time in 1998, was he the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998, he was the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. We were there when he took his oath in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether at this time while he was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in 1998, who was a member of the Supreme Defence Council on behalf of Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Milo Djukanovic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let us first have a look at a document. It's a document from the OTP 65 ter list 8238. Could we please have a look at the last page of the document so that we could see who the author is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can see here that document was drafted on the 23rd of July, 1998, and signed by the Chief of General Staff, General Perisic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please go back to the first page so that we could see who this document was addressed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are leaving us all behind, sir. We are still being taken to the last page to see who signed it, you were already on date back at the first page. We haven't seen who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we then please bring back the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now if we could please go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can see that this is a letter addressed to the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Mr. Slobodan Milosevic. First of all, I will ask you, are you familiar with this letter, General?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now that I'm reading it, I remember all the positions expressed in it. This is what we were opposing. The personnel policy, violation of the usual chain of command and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the interpreter would like you to please repeat the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2 in B/C/S, please, and I think it is also page 2 in English that I wish to present.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please read item 1 for yourself. I do not wish to go into details too much. And down here it says "Proposed Solution," can you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's the last paragraph. Can we please bring up the document a little bit so that we can see the bottom part in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Use legally -- let me just read it out, or let me not read it. What is the gist of this?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the army be used, the first paragraph is our typical position that the army should be used legally only for the defence of the border area, military facilities, units, if they are under attack, and that all other tasks should be carried out by other organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please just turn to the next page in English, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under number 2 here, General, what is it here you just described it a while ago?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Guards Brigade is a unit from the Special Forces corps and is directly subordinated to the Chief of General Staff, and according to the institution and according to the law, there was no single unit that could be separated from the army and then subordinated directly to the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did Milosevic do that?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the president did just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please turn to the next page in B/C/S. It is something that the Trial Chamber can already see under item 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I would ask you to comment on what paragraph 3 contains.

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The proposal was just not to allow the army to be commanded outside of the military subordination, outside of the knowledge of the General Staff, outside of the command of the 3rd Army which had a forward command post in Pristina, that levels should not be overlooked when tasks were issued to units. So it was with good intentions and in good faith that the Chief of General Staff propose to the president that this should be eliminated. He also reminded him of the rules of service and informed him that we knew that he was doing it without the knowledge of the Chief of General Staff and in contravention to the military subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we also now have a look at the very end of the document and comment on the last paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the last paragraph, General.

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have had a look at it. That was the last warning to the president that the Chief of General Staff would be uncompromising in preserving the unity of the army and in building the army according to the principles that we had set out, and that he would not participate in violating the principles on which military organisation as such is based.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D498. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As we know that the NATO campaign in Kosovo began in March 1999, at the time while General Perisic was still the Chief of General Staff, what was his position about the serious nature of in intervention, that there would really be a NATO intervention in Kosovo? So what was the position taken by General Perisic and other members of the collegium?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the month of October 1998, it was clear to us from talks with international representatives and also on the basis of our own assessments that NATO would intervene in Kosovo and Metohija unless the manner of resolving problems in Kosovo were changed, and unless the president abandoned the policy of opposing the international community. We believed that the time that was already set for October was postponed until March and that within this period the change of our position and our policy should take place. Our position was that President Milosevic had to make a compromise at a certain moment and thus not allow for any bomb or any explosive device to fall on the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia because we believed that this would be the worst possible outcome and result.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you tell this to President Milosevic, this position and your assessment?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I don't know what exactly the Chief of General Staff did later on after he was replaced as a general who remained within the General Staff. Just before the new year 1999 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just stop you there, Mr. Borovic. The question is: Did you tell this to President Milosevic, this position and your assessment. Could you try and answer that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to answer that. I wrote this position and addressed it to General Ojdanic in a six-page document, but as I believe that General Ojdanic would not react to this and would not inform President Milosevic about it, I used the same document but without the stamp, the military school centre stamps. I gave it over to Minister Cerovic who was a member of JUL, that is to say the Yugoslav Left. He was a member of the main board of this political party. He was very close to President Milosevic and his family. So I handed it over to him, asking him to hand it over directly to the president and I told him that this was our latest position, the position of the people who were -- who made up the last composition of the office of the Chief of General Staff. I know that Minister Cerovic did hand this over to President Milosevic, but after that in March the NATO intervention began and this was not accepted. Later on, I came into possession of this document, a copy of it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you now about the replacement. What was it that happened in November 1998 in Gornji Milanovac? Were you there?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, time passed by and the president wasn't changing anything in his policy, in his overall conduct. The Chief of General Staff organised the visit to the town of Gornji Milanovac, probably because it was his home-town and I was part of that delegation. After we visited a factory, the chief was supposed to have a conference with the leadership of the municipality and with the prominent businessmen from that area. The Chief of General Staff was unusual bold in his public statements about the problems that he was encountering, the army was encountering, and the state as such, and he even questioned the extent to which such a state was capable of putting up a defence. And he stated certain views and assessments that we in the delegation shared but had never expressed publicly. We were quite taken aback by this openness of the chief on this occasion. I knew that there would be ripples after this event and there would be consequences for the chief and I tried to prevent that. I remained with the cameramen and the reporters and I took all this material from them to stop them from broadcasting, but still I knew there were many people in that conference hall, also people from the SPS party and the president would certainly find out. With the rest of the delegation, the Chief of General Staff travelled on to a small place nearby called Vlasenica which is the birth place of a famous poet of ours, and I stayed behind to do some damage control and prevent this material from going out into the public. When we met up again and talked, I told him that it's going to be bad for us, and then we returned to Belgrade where there was already a reception going on in a congress centre. The president was there with his wife. We greeted him and then followed the reactions that ultimately he led to the replacement of General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we just -- so it was General Perisic who was talking at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if General Perisic was appointed to a new position, something to do with the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know. He was given a fictional position of advisor to the federal prime minister for something or other.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the views of Milo Djukanovic from Montenegro, a member of the Supreme Defence Council on the replacement of General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew. I knew from General Perisic and from the Chef de Cabinet that Milo Djukanovic was firmly against the replacement of General Perisic and if the constitution had been fully respected, the decision could not have been made without a consensus, but still General Perisic was replaced by General Ojdanic and given a new mostly fictive position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you give us the date when this took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't tell you the date but there was a session of the Supreme Defence Council recording that and you can find the date there. I saw General Perisic the very next day in the centre for military schools, and I can tell you about it, but I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in November --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Early November, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just about to call up that document, 65 ter 01178D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see on the screen this record of the session of the Supreme Defence Council held on 24 November 1998. We see who was there. It was chaired by the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Slobodan Milosevic, and there were the president of Serbia, Milan Milutinovic, and president of Montenegro, Milo Djukanovic. And also there was Slavoljub Susic who we mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 3 in B/C/S called "Personnel Issues."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This first paragraph said: "Opening the session, opening the debate on personnel issues in the Yugoslav Army, President Slobodan Milosevic pointed out the necessity to replace the Chief of General Staff in view of the fact that Lieutenant-General Momcilo Perisic had been occupying that duty for an unusually long time." It seems to be some sort of statement of reasons. Do you know that this was at the time Milosevic's argument for replacing Perisic, at least officially?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just pro forma. He had to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's turn the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's where we see what President Milo Djukanovic of Montenegro --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the next page in English, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this second paragraph of Djukanovic's contribution, it says he is not in favour of changing the current Chief of General Staff of the Yugoslav Army, General Perisic, regardless of his long occupation of that post. According to President Djukanovic, General Perisic has proven authority and great experience --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move to the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- while he was still Chief of General Staff. What was the relationship between General Perisic and the leadership of Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time the relations were good. I happen to know that General Perisic and General Aco Dimitrijevic did not believe at the time that the leadership of Montenegro had cessationist ambitions. They did not want to leave the union with Serbia and the Federation of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us remain with that page in B/C/S, but in English we need the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's the paragraph at the top of the English page to see what Milutinovic had to say: "As far as the good international reputation enjoyed by Perisic, one should take that with a grain of salt and not pay too much attention. We will deal with our own affairs, Internal Affairs, as we see best." What kind of international reputation was he talking about? What was Milutinovic trying to say?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all later contacts with the ministers that we had, General Perisic was very balanced in his views in all he said, and the impression he left was extremely good and that also applied to the contacts with international representatives. I also accompanied him to one meeting with Geneva. He was an operational thinker and he always guessed -- Milutinovic always guessed in advance the opinion of President Milosevic and what he wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just see the last page in B/C/S. It must be the last page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I won't read the first two paragraphs aloud because they are long, but please read them to yourself, especially the conclusions. And what follows from this position that Milosevic is taking?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that it reflects the general position of Milosevic. He would always consult us and he would always seem to agree with us but then he would decide whatever he pleased as if no consultations had taken place, and you can see that he did the same here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At this session we see that Lieutenant-General Dragoljub Ojdanic was appointed as new Chief of the General Staff, and Momcilo Perisic was appointed advisor to the government for defence issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D499. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened after this cabinet meeting? What was the reaction of General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Perisic came to see me at the centre of military schools. He had prepared a statement for the press which was accurate but too sharp and too dry without any reasons explained. And I tried to rewrite it producing another two drafts to address these issues, but the general refused to change anything and he just said in his statement that he is leaving his position and he is placing himself at the disposal of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 01130D is the next document we need.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General Perisic says here: "The current authorities do not like leaders who are men of integrity. I was dismissed from my duties as Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army without any consultation in an inappropriate and illegal manner. I do not accept the made-up position that I was offered in the current federal government. I remain at the disposal of my army, the state, and the people." Is that the text of his press statement?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that day, did anything else happen at the centre for military schools when he came to see you?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Perisic asked me whether I would allow him to address the cadets and the officers undergoing training in that school in any class for him to present his views and he warned me that I might suffer consequences if I allow him to do that. I answered that he is the Chief of General Staff, he has the right to visit any school and address our students even at the highest-ranking school that we had, and that was the national defence school. General Perisic addressed the national defence school, but I did not attend his address because in principle I never attended anyone's address to students except when I was monitoring those classes. So I told him that he was free to tell them whatever he wished. After that there were reactions against me from the minister, the Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What were these reactions like?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly threatening that I shouldn't have allowed without consulting the Chief of General Staff and without asking for the approval of the minister for this to happen, so I was threatened with being sanctioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time you were assistant to the Chief of General Staff of the Yugoslav Army for education, training --

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also scientific research and publication activities of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Soon after that you became the chief of the technical administration for the logistics sector of the Yugoslav Army. So let me now ask you in the military hierarchy, were you promoted or demoted?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was demoted, of course. I was appointed to a lower duty as compared to the one that I held previously. So my further promotion was blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would seek to tender this document into evidence, Your Honour. And I think that now we have reached a round number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have reached a round number?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just referring to the number itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D500. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the last question, General: Do you know if you had any contact with General Perisic when he became aware of the indictment of ICTY and do you know what was his position vis-a-vis this indictment?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in touch with the general and I was aware of his position. He was clear as always, he said, I would not hide from anything or anyone. Once I receive the summon, I will go there and I will answer before the Court for everything I ever did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see 65 ter 01015D from the Defence 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, do you know what this is?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know and it's well known to everyone. This is the statement which General Momcilo Perisic, now a retired general, issued on the occasion of the issuance of the indictment against him in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would seek to tender this document into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D501. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have finished my direct examination, General, Professor Borovic, and I wish to thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I just need a moment to set up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, General Borovic.

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is now my opportunity to ask you some questions about your testimony and I will first of all, I'd like to clarify any ambiguity in your testimony, and that is, the date when you were appointed chief of the cabinet of General Perisic. At page 13881, line 21, you testified that that was in November of 1994, and at page 13900, line 20, Mr. Lukic, in a question, indicated that you had become the Chef de Cabinet in December of 1994 and you didn't correct that. So my question to you is, when was the date that you became the Chef de Cabinet?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the correct date is as I was speaking from memory, Mr. Lukic has my personnel file in which one can see the exact date, so 15 or 20 years later, I cannot remember the exact date, but my CV and my personnel file, which is available, includes the date and I believe that the information provided by Attorney Lukic is the relevant one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So you believe you started the position of Chef de Cabinet in December of 1994?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the information included in my personnel file is exact. There you can see when this duty was handed over to me and when I received it, as far as I can remember it seems to me that it was in November, but I cannot be certain about the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Unfortunately, General, I don't have your personnel file so I have to rely on your evidence. Now, let me clarify another point that you testified about and that is Prosecution Exhibit 2729. You are testified about that exhibit, testimony is found at page 13999 and starts at line 18, and I just want to get a point of clarification on this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have this exhibit on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You see this document, General? You recall this is a document that is dated the 23rd of June, 1995. It was sent from the VJ -- office of the VJ General Staff to the Republika Srpska Main Staff to General Mladic, and it deals with 400 men led by Colonel Trku lja to be sent. What I'm interested in is the next page of the B/C/S of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn to the second page of B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this page is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we on the first page in the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we remain on the first page of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is the second page of the B/C/S version. First of all, sir, can you identify the handwriting and can you identify the initials at the end of this document?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I do recognise the handwriting as well as the initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Whose handwriting is it and whose initials are they?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's General Perisic's handwriting and these are his initials, MP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we look it at the -- back to the first page in the Serbian language text, did you prepare this document, General?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was drafted at the office. I sent it out to be encrypted and to the Main Staff of the army. The contents was just copied from the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That was my point that I wanted to clarify. In other words, the procedure was General Perisic in response to this request drafted in his own hand a response that was then reproduced by a member of your staff and sent on to General Mladic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me explore with you for a moment the issue of official army notebooks. Is there a procedure in the VJ, and was there a procedure at the time General Perisic was chief of the VJ General Staff, that an official army notebook would be issued to him?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Official army notebooks were documents which each officer of the Yugoslav Army had and so did the Chief of General Staff. It was a certified notebook with a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe the procedure of maintaining the notebook and the procedure that was implemented when one reached the last page of the notebook?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a working notebook of each officer and chief to be used for their personal needs and once it was filled out, it would be handed over to be filed in the archives or it was destroyed depending on the importance of the level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say, sir, that this was for their personal needs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they were recorded as the personal notebooks of officers and I never handed over those that I used to the archives. They were all destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the end --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But my question is: Did you say they were for personal needs, were they not for official army work? Didn't you have to record in there what you did for the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was the purpose, but each person had it to record his own personal duties, so they were not used for their needs outside of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Their personal duties, not personal needs? You see earlier you were interpreted as saying, this is at page 26, line 22: "It was a working notebook of each officer and chief to be used for the personal needs and once it was filled out, it would be handed over to be filed in the archives or it was destroyed, depending on the importance of the level." Now, that's why I wanted to find out whether is this for your personal needs, is this a personal diary, like my own diary that I have personally, making dates with my friends?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, meetings would be recorded but only what related to the army, so the person could jot down his own diary entries or impressions if there was anything to note, but that was an official army notebook. When I said personal needs, I meant that it was personally used by the person to whom it was issued and it included information that was of interest for the army, not information from private life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time. I can continue with this topic after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take the break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may the record show that Judge Picard has now joined the Chamber, and we are no longer sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General, we were talking about Official Note books maintained by General Perisic. During the time that you were his Chef de Cabinet, did General Perisic in fact have officially-issued VJ notebooks?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Perisic had an official VJ notebook. We had two kinds of notebooks, an official one in peacetime and a war notebook for war time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Since there was no war time at the time you were Chef de Cabinet in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, let me address the type of notebook that was maintained during peacetime because that's the type we are talking about, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I just mentioned that the other document was also part of the obligatory equipment that every commanding officer had in his back-pack.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how large those notebooks were? How many pages were contained in one of those notebooks?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those notebooks were of the A5 format. They had between 100 and 200 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When one exhausted the 100 to 200 pages, sir, tell us exactly what the protocol was in respect of the notebook?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was always returned to the organ which had issued it. That was the general affairs service and the archives, and then their commission would further decide whether it would be kept and archived or destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the end of each official notebook when one concluded the 100 to 200 pages, was there a certification stamp placed at the end of the notebook before it was turned over to the general affairs people?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not certified by any stamp that that was the end. The officer in question would simply hand it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And how many -- to the best of your recollection, sir, while you were Chef de Cabinet, how many official notebooks did General Perisic complete?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I do not remember how many notebooks he had filled in but he wrote quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In addition to the official notebook that you've described, did he keep a personal notebook?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, as far as I know and as far as I knew General Perisic, he did not keep any personal notes or a personal diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were General Perisic's completed VJ notebooks turned over to the general affairs, I think you said general affairs organs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Services.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- services?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we handed them over to the office archives and then the archivists dealt with it further. I'm not even aware of the exact procedure, I just know that there is a service for documentation which issues these notebooks and takes care of them, but I don't know what happened with these notebooks later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when you say they were handed over to archivist, can you be more explicit on that. Which archivist, the army archivist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the witness already answered, but it has not been recorded this part of the sentence that Mr. Harmon is now asking him to state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If it's not recorded, can we then hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had the archives within the office and archivist, so we would hand it over to the office archives and the archives office kept everything from the office that was supposed to be kept. And then what we didn't keep within those archives, they would hand it over to the army archives which is a more general service, but I don't know what was the criteria for sending something there because there was a special service or administration for archiving materials and documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You say that your office kept everything from the office. While you were -- through your term as Chef de Cabinet, were General Perisic's notebooks maintained in your office?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should have been like that, but I don't know exactly whether they were kept at the office or forwarded somewhere else to be kept, but we always handed them over to the office archives. All the documents that were within the competence of the Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you have any idea today where those official VJ notebooks of General Perisic's are?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the witness previously answered. Let me just see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, if you remember, Mr. Harmon, the witness did say they were handed over, he didn't know happened to them. I'm not quite sure whether if he didn't know then he would know today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's possible, Your Honour, between the intervening period of time he may have seen one or more of those notebooks and that's what I'm attempting to explore with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe if you ask him in that sharpened manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Since you left your position as the Chef de Cabinet of the VJ General Staff, have you seen any of General Perisic's notebooks between the period you left and today?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor, I never saw any of the documents including General Perisic's notebooks after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn to Prosecution Exhibit 2746, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document about which you testified. It is a document that is dated the 7th of October, 1995. It is a document from the VRS Main Staff to General Perisic personally requesting ten air-bombs. You testified yesterday or the day before about the procedure that would be used in terms of dealing with such a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 2 of the English and if we could scroll to the bottom of the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, there's two points in respect of this document I'd like to explore with you, sir. The first is the procedure, and as I understand the procedure, when you received this request, you forwarded this request on to the air force and anti-aircraft defence sector; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: They would then consider the request and make a determination of whether or not there was sufficient materiels available to comply with the request; correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I assume, General, that the head of the sector was not the person who would do the analysis of whether materiels were available. I assume, sir, that this manner would be referred to the sector's technical department for an analysis, and then that analysis would be provided to the head of the sector and the head of the sector would then forward his response to you; is that how it worked?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is how it worked but not the technical centre, rather the administration who was technically in charge of materiel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Did that have any specific name within the branch of the air force and anti-aircraft defence sector?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the administration for air force. A sector has a number of administrations who are tactically in charge, so there was an administration that was in charge of the air force and anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now, the other item, just to fully complete an analysis of this document. You testified yesterday that this document -- you were shown this document and then you were shown P951 which was a document referring to the collection of air-bombs from the 608th Logistical Base, but for completeness sake I want to focus on this request specifically since you did not mention who approved the request for these air-bombs. Can you tell us who approved this request for air-bombs?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Chief of General Staff believed that the request should be approved and resolved, but he needed feedback from the RV and PVO sector, and here this feedback is requested whether this can be resolved and how. I suppose that after this feedback from the RV and PVO sector was indeed received.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we take a look at the bottom of the Serbian language, there's some text there which indicates the Chief of the General Staff VJ has approved for the General Staff VRS to be resolved as soon as possible. And he asked that a reply be sent. I take it, General, that General Perisic would have been the person who approved the provision of these air-bombs to the VRS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this case, the chief accepted the request and approved that this sector should deal with it if possible, that's why I asked for feedback. Obviously something important was at stake. He accepted the request and approved that it be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. On page 34, line 10, he -- the witness said he asked this sector to resolve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So let's get a clarification on your last sentence, General Borovic. Mr. Lukic is suggesting that the transcript is incorrect. It currently reads: "He accepted the request and approved that it be resolved." Was that what you said or did you say something else?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said he approved the request and asked the sector for air force and aircraft -- anti-aircraft defence to resolve it and to provide feedback because he couldn't deal with it himself because he didn't know if these assets were available in the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't want to belabour this point, but did he get feedback from the air force and anti-aircraft defence in respect of this specific request?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know off the cuff, but if he is asking for feedback, then feedback was supposed to come through the office to the chief. It must be in the documentation. I don't know whether it's there, but I believe feedback must have come eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And can we conclude that by the provision of these documents and you saw a document yesterday, it was Prosecution Exhibit 951, saying that the air-bombs could be collected from the 608th Logistics Base that after receiving that feedback General Perisic would have approved this request?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to clarify a point that was raised earlier this morning in your evidence. This morning at page 8 of the LiveNote, Mr. Lukic asked you a question and the question was the following: "Do you remember while you were still working as Chef de Cabinet and later on did General Perisic consider the possibility of leaving this position not resigning" - these are the words I want to focus on - "because you cannot resign in the army, but abandoning this duty as Chief of General Staff?" Now, isn't it a fact, sir, that under Article 107 of the Law on the Army, that military service of a professional officer or a non-commissioned officer shall be terminated, and then subpart 6 reads, at his own request?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be terminated at his own request, but a request may also be made for him to be transferred to another duty within the Army of Yugoslavia. There was no such thing as resignation for an officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I refer, Your Honours, to P197. It is Article 107 and I don't take the matter any further than that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This morning you testified about General Perisic and elements relating to his resignation. The Kosovo crisis was a crisis that confronted the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and needed to be addressed both diplomatically, politically, and militarily; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is precisely the nature of the Kosovo crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, sir, on the 24th of June, 1998, General Perisic requested -- made a request for a feasibility and method of engaging -- engagement of peacetime forces in Kosovo; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was Grom 98?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the Grom 98 assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me see if I can refresh your recollection, sir. On the 28th of July, did General Perisic issue a directive to the commands of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd Army, to the air force anti-aircraft defence, to the navy, and to the special units corps to deploy the Yugoslav Army for securing the state border with Albania, units and facilities in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, and crush the armed rebel forces; do you remember that directive, sir?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998 I was not aware of those documents. I was at the centre of military schools, but it sounds logical to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You commented earlier today on the letter that General Perisic addressed to President Milosevic, it was D498, in which he complained about the use of the army. That letter was dated the 23rd of July, 1998. The directive that was issued by General Perisic was five days later. It's dated the 28th of July, 1998. Do you accept that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said very positively that he didn't know anything about that directive. I think this question is going beyond that context and we will ultimately get into pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say -- are you saying if a document is dated the 28th of July, 1998 and another one is dated the 23rd of July, 1998, you are speculating if you answer that whether it came five days later? Is that speculation? Or is it simple arithmetic? Listen to the question: Do you accept that this letter was written five days later?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at least the witness could be shown that document. How can he accept anything about it if he hasn't seen it. That's the point of my objection. The witness does not know anything about one of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If the premise is it's dated the 28th of July, then it's a question of simple arithmetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not include this on my notification to the Defence because it only came up during the direct examination this morning, so I will, with the Court's permission, I will ask that this be uploaded into e-court and I will then show it to the witness so we can confirm the date on this directive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This will be uploaded General, you'll have an opportunity to inspect the document and inspect the date. Sir, the issue, the point of departure between General Perisic and President Milosevic wasn't whether forces, Yugoslav Army forces should be engaged in Kosovo, it was that there had not been a state of war declared, and, therefore, forces could not legally be deployed, wasn't that the point of departure and difference between President Milosevic and General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not the only difference. Differences started before between them and they had do with the whole concept of engaging the army in Kosovo. I just said that from that letter that I am aware was sent to Milosevic, I am aware of the views that we had discussed earlier with the general and he put them down in that letter. All that is in the letter, that that was the difference between him and Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So that was a point of difference between Milosevic and General Perisic was that the army could not legally be engaged in Kosovo without a declaration of war?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's one of the points of difference, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And notwithstanding that difference, General Perisic prepared a directive by engaging the Yugoslav Army in Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how this developed later, so I can't say whether you are right or not. I don't have these documents and I haven't seen them in proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, until this is uploaded I'll go to a different subject --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But before you leave this subject, Mr. Harmon, I would think I would like to go back to the question you asked the witness earlier and I want to read it to you. You said: "Let me see if I can refresh your recollection, sir. On the 28th of July, did General Perisic issue a directive to the commands of the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Army, to the air force anti-aircraft defence, to the navy, and to the special units corps to deploy the Yugoslav Army for securing the state border with Albania, units and facilities in the territory of the Kosovo and Metohija and crush the armed rebel forces; do you remember that?" Now, I think we've heard evidence that it is the responsibility of the army to look after the borders, the national borders. Now, I don't -- are you not making a distinction between securing the border and taking an act of aggression in another country?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm merely pointing out that there is a war -- a plan, a directive, that was issued to the forces, and it is a plan that is for purposes of obviously securing the territory, including Kosovo and Metohija. And that's the point I'm trying to make with this witness. The name -- the directive is securing the border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I accept that. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But securing the border -- and that's my question. Are you not making a distinction between securing the border and going to war?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Because I think you are now asking the witness that General Perisic ordered the army to go to war without a state of war having been declared.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this directive discusses what each of the armies, each of the subordinate units is required to do in -- let's find the right page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm only relying on the question you asked earlier, you know, securing the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, but that's the caption of the document I'm going to show the witness. The witness can explain it obviously if he sees it and he can better explain it. But this is a document that discusses the engagement of the Yugoslav forces in respect of the events in Kosovo. The point I was trying to make with this witness is that General Perisic was not opposed to the use of the Yugoslav Army forces in Kosovo. He had -- and I raise this with the witness, the point of difference was a legal difference, a technical difference, that there was no state of war declared, and therefore the use of the army would be illegal under those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was Kosovo a territory of former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It was part of the former Yugoslavia, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Clear it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am sorry, I didn't hear it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Clear it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Explain to us sir, the state of Kosovo, what its relationship was to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kosovo was an integral part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It was an autonomous province within the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll return to this subject when I have this document uploaded and after the break I'll return to this subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hate to disrupt, but would I like to suggest, if Mr. Harmon doesn't mind, that the witness be given a copy during the break to look through the entire document because the witness is saying he is not aware of this document, perhaps Mr. Harmon could agree to let the witness have a copy during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's a good suggestion, Your Honour. I have no objection to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, on the first day of your evidence, you testified about delegations, military delegations and along with certain political representatives travelling to Russia and to Hungary. You discussed P476.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could have that on the monitor, please. Defence 476, I'm sorry. On the monitor, just to refresh your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This was one of the items that you discussed. This was a meeting in Russia with the head of the Russian General Staff, General Grachev, and it was attended by the federal minister of defence, Bulatovic. Did any other representatives of the VJ attend this particular meeting in Russia?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is one of the drafts of this document. The Chief of the General Staff was present, I was present, I believe the Chef de Cabinet of Pavle Bulatovic was also there, but I'm not sure, and the interpreter. We had prepared the military aspect of that visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You indicated in your testimony that this was in 1995. Can you recall the month when this was in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the month, but winter had just started in Moscow, but it's in the documentation in the reports about the visit. This is just one of the drafts of the agreement bearing no date. If I had known the date would be necessary, I would have prepared it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I take it when delegations, military delegations went to foreign countries to conduct business with them, such as the visit to Russia and the visited to Hungary that you described, these meetings were attended by the highest-ranking members of the Yugoslav Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we take a look at D477, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This -- while we are waiting for it to come up on the monitor, General, this is the document that describes your February 2nd, 1995, visit to Hungary to meet with the General Staff of the Hungarian army. And we can see in this document in the second full paragraph of the document that the Yugoslav Army delegation was composed of General Perisic, who was the Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army, Lieutenant-General Mile Mrksic, Lieutenant-General Ljubisa Velickovic, Colonel Branko Krga, yourself, and Lieutenant Jusuf Banjica. Let me just ask you, I think you identified General Ljubisa Velickovic this morning in your testimony. He was the head of air force and anti-aircraft defence? Is that correct? He was the chief of that sector?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of air force and anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Branko Krga, was he chief of 2nd administration, in other words, the intelligence administration of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: An General Mile Mrksic, what was his position on 2nd of February, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was assistant of the Chief of General Staff for ground forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Mile Mrksic, are you aware that approximately two weeks later, Mile Mrksic was appointed as an advisor to the federal minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that but I don't know it in such precise terms. I know that he was transferred to the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And after he went to the federal Ministry of Defence, he was transferred to the -- become the commander of the SVK, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And as a result of his actions, or, perhaps inactions, in the Republika Srpska Krajina, he was retroactively retired from the Yugoslav Army, retroactively to the 30th of December, 1994; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when he was retroactively retired. Generals were promoted and retired without the knowledge of the office of the Chief of General Staff. All that was within the purview of the Supreme Defence Council and it was handled by the assistant for legal and personnel affairs. I don't know about that line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why don't we discuss your evidence that you gave in respect of General Perisic meeting with General Mladic. You testified that General Perisic met at the General Staff three times. What can you tell us, General, about General Mladic's visits to Perisic before General Perisic assumed the position of chief -- I am sorry, before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would appreciate a reference for the page where the witness stated that Perisic had met Mladic three times at the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That reference is found at page 13928. It starts at line 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, sir, what can you tell us about General Mladic's visits to the General Staff prior to your becoming Chef de Cabinet?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything about it. I don't know whether he had come before that. I first heard of General Mladic when General Djukic was leaving. Until then I didn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you on your feet, Mr. Lukic? Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had a problem with the transcript over the past few days and I'm now looking for references. The question of Mr. Harmon was that the witness said that General Perisic had seen General Mladic on the premises of the General Staff three times, and the transcript I have in front of me, page 55, line 9, it's an unrevised transcript and Mr. Harmon will tell me if that's what he meant. My question was --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can refer counsel to page 13928. Mr. Lukic asked the question: "Did you have occasion to meet with General Mladic on his visits to the General Staff?" The witness answered: "Perhaps two or three times." And he describes in his answer, which I will now go into with the witness, those three occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the point of my objection. The witness answered me that he was present at three meetings, not that General Perisic met with General Mladic three times on the premises of the General Staff, which is the suggestion made in Mr. Harmon's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then I can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
